title: Two Routes, One Patch of Skin

scenes.tts: Press the skin of a mouse's hindpaw. How does the news reach the brainstem? The textbook draws one route. There are two.
scenes.visual: Title card: Two Routes, One Patch of Skin. A mouse hindpaw; a small blunt probe, 1 mm across, presses one patch of skin, which glows (schematic, not to scale). Question on screen: how does the news reach the brainstem?
scenes.narration: Press the skin of a mouse's hindpaw. How does the news reach the brainstem? The textbook draws one route. There are two.

scenes.tts: Start with the textbook drawing. A touch afferent, an A beta low-threshold mechanoreceptor, enters the spinal cord. Its main branch climbs the dorsal column on the same side.
scenes.caption: Start with the textbook drawing. A touch afferent, an Aβ low-threshold mechanoreceptor, enters the spinal cord. Its main branch climbs the dorsal column on the same side.
scenes.visual: Cross-section of the cord: grey butterfly, dorsal horn at the top, white-matter dorsal column above it. A blue axon enters from the dorsal root and turns upward in the dorsal column. Label: touch afferent (Aβ low-threshold mechanoreceptor).
scenes.narration: Start with the textbook drawing. A touch afferent, an Aβ low-threshold mechanoreceptor, enters the spinal cord. Its main branch climbs the dorsal column on the same side.

scenes.tts: It reaches the gracile nucleus in the brainstem with no synapse on the way. Call this the direct route.
scenes.visual: Camera follows the blue axon up a long cord to the caudal medulla, where it ends on a gracile neuron. Label: gracile nucleus. Tag on the blue line: direct route, no synapse.
scenes.narration: It reaches the gracile nucleus in the brainstem with no synapse on the way. Call this the direct route.

scenes.tts: Now look below that drawing. The same afferent also sends branches into the dorsal horn, a layered circuit.
scenes.visual: Back to the lumbar cross-section, enlarged. A side branch of the blue afferent dips into the dorsal horn. Label: lumbar dorsal horn.
scenes.narration: Now look below that drawing. The same afferent also sends branches into the dorsal horn, a layered circuit.

scenes.tts: Those branches drive local interneurons. Through them, and in places directly, they drive a spinal neuron whose own axon climbs the same dorsal column.
scenes.visual: The dorsal horn shows faint layers; small interneurons light up around the branch's terminals. Gold arrows: afferent branch to interneurons to one larger spinal neuron, plus one thinner arrow straight from the afferent branch to that neuron. That neuron's gold axon turns up into the dorsal column beside the blue one.
scenes.narration: Those branches drive local interneurons. Through them, and in places directly, they drive a spinal neuron whose own axon climbs the same dorsal column.

scenes.tts: This is a postsynaptic dorsal column neuron, or P S D C neuron. It is driven in the dorsal horn and projects to the brainstem.
scenes.caption: This is a postsynaptic dorsal column neuron, or PSDC neuron. It is driven in the dorsal horn and projects to the brainstem.
scenes.visual: The gold neuron is ringed. On screen: postsynaptic dorsal column (PSDC) neuron = driven in the dorsal horn, axon up the dorsal column.
scenes.narration: This is a postsynaptic dorsal column neuron, or PSDC neuron. It is driven in the dorsal horn and projects to the brainstem.

scenes.tts: Recordings in cats described these neurons by the early nineteen eighties. Mouse work adds genetic access, and a test of each route.
scenes.caption: Recordings in cats described these neurons by the early 1980s. Mouse work adds genetic access, and a test of each route.
scenes.visual: Small inset: a cat silhouette beside an older-style spike trace, label: cat recordings, by the early 1980s. The inset swaps to a mouse with two small switch icons. Label: genetic access; test each route.
scenes.narration: Recordings in cats described these neurons by the early 1980s. Mouse work adds genetic access, and a test of each route.

scenes.tts: So draw a second line, in gold, from the afferent through the circuit and up to the gracile nucleus.
scenes.visual: The full gold line traces from paw to dorsal horn to PSDC neuron and up the dorsal column, running beside the blue line toward the medulla.
scenes.narration: So draw a second line, in gold, from the afferent through the circuit and up to the gracile nucleus.

scenes.tts: Pause and predict. Does the gold line end on the same brainstem neurons as the blue line?
scenes.visual: The gold line's tip hovers just below the gracile nucleus. Two ghosted options: one gracile neuron shared with the blue line, or a separate neuron. Question on screen.
scenes.narration: Pause and predict. Does the gold line end on the same brainstem neurons as the blue line?

scenes.tts: For thalamus-projecting gracile neurons, yes. The two inputs had highly aligned receptive fields. Both reported the same patch of skin.
scenes.visual: The gold line lands on the same gracile neuron as the blue line. Label: thalamus-projecting gracile neuron. Below, the hindpaw: the blue and gold receptive fields overlap on one patch.
scenes.narration: For thalamus-projecting gracile neurons, yes. The two inputs had highly aligned receptive fields. Both reported the same patch of skin.

scenes.tts: But the two reports are not the same. The direct route keeps precise timing. The indirect route reports sustained pressure, up to high forces.
scenes.visual: Blue line tagged with a crisp, regularly spaced spike train: precise timing. Gold line tagged with a long steady bar of firing during a held press: sustained pressure, up to high forces.
scenes.narration: But the two reports are not the same. The direct route keeps precise timing. The indirect route reports sustained pressure, up to high forces.

scenes.tts: That is the idea for this lesson. Two routes, one patch of skin. One report keeps the timing. The other is rebuilt in the cord, not copied.
scenes.visual: On screen: Two routes, one patch of skin. Blue = direct, keeps timing. Gold = rebuilt in the dorsal horn, reports sustained pressure. A crossed-out label over the gold line: delayed copy. Both meet on one gracile neuron.
scenes.narration: That is the idea for this lesson. Two routes, one patch of skin. One report keeps the timing. The other is rebuilt in the cord, not copied.

scenes.tts: The limits: these are mouse studies, mostly in anaesthetized adults, and the dorsal column route only.
scenes.visual: Scope card with three short lines: mouse hindlimb; mostly anaesthetized adults; dorsal column route only.
scenes.narration: The limits: these are mouse studies, mostly in anaesthetized adults, and the dorsal column route only.

scenes.tts: The takeaway: one touch, two routes, two different reports on the same skin.
scenes.visual: The two lines rejoin on one gracile neuron above the one glowing patch of skin. Takeaway on screen: one touch, two routes, two different reports on the same skin.
scenes.narration: The takeaway: one touch, two routes, two different reports on the same skin.
